# The OpenScript library, every name

Read from `openalgo-script@0.5.0`, the compiler this app ships, so it is
what the browser will actually accept. `coverage.mjs` holds this page to the
compiler in both directions: a name the compiler has and this page lacks fails,
and so does a name here the compiler does not have.

**350 names across 13 groups, and 19 colours.**

95 of them are **planned and not implemented in this version**, and are
marked. The library describes a name whether or not a version implements it, so
a name being here is not a promise that it compiles: reaching for one is OS2020,
which names it and says so. These were measured by putting every name to this
compiler rather than by keeping a list beside it.

## How to read the warmup column

A stateful call answers nothing until it has seen enough bars. `sma(close, 20)`
is absent on bars 0 to 18 and first answers on bar 19. That absence propagates:
arithmetic on an absent value is absent, and it is **not** zero. A script that
assumes a number during warmup is quietly wrong for its first stretch of bars,
which is the single most common way a ported study disagrees with its original.

`bar 0` means it answers from the first bar and has no warmup.

| `bar.isConfirmed` | This bar's interval has elapsed and it will not change again | bar 0 |
| `bar.isFirst` | This is the oldest bar supplied | bar 0 |
| `bar.isLast` | This is the newest bar supplied | bar 0 |
| `bar.isNew` | The last update appended a bar rather than replacing one | bar 0 |
| `bar.isRealtime` | A live feed is driving updates, rather than a one-off history load | bar 0 |
| `bar.updates` | How many times this bar has been executed | bar 0 |

## Colours

Named constants, usable anywhere a colour is taken. A colour carries its own
transparency, so these can be faded rather than replaced.

`aqua`, `black`, `blue`, `brown`, `fuchsia`, `gray`, `green`, `lime`, `maroon`, `navy`, `olive`, `orange`, `pink`, `purple`, `red`, `silver`, `teal`, `white`, `yellow`.

## The calls marked not portable

The transcendental family is computed by the host's own maths library, which is
correct to about one unit in the last place and differs between platforms in
that last bit. The language specification has no reference algorithm for them
yet, so two engines running the same script may differ in the final digit of a
result that reaches one.

They work, and they compute what they have always computed. What they do not
carry is a guarantee that a backtest run on one machine and a live run on
another agree to the last bit. For most scripts that is irrelevant; for one
whose signal turns on a comparison at that precision, it is not.
